sections.h2: Who handles property tax in Iroquois County?
sections.html:
Two offices in the Iroquois County Administrative Center at 1001 East Grant Street in Watseka share the work. The Treasurer, in Room 105, bills and collects the tax and can be reached at (815) 432-6985. The Assessment Office, in Room 106, handles values, exemptions and appeals at (815) 432-6978. Both post Monday through Friday hours that end at 4:30 in the afternoon.

A three-member Board of Review sits apart from the assessor's staff and decides assessment complaints on the evidence shown at hearing. Township assessors in the county's townships handle first-line questions about a parcel's record.

  • Bills, payments and tax sale questions: the County Treasurer.
  • Exemptions, property record cards and address changes: the Assessment Office, where deputy clerks answer record requests by email.
  • Assessment complaints: the Board of Review, using the county's complaint form.
  • Tax rates: the County Clerk's Office.

sections.h2: What is Iroquois County like for someone selling a house?
sections.html:
Iroquois County lies along the Indiana line in northeast Illinois, with its northern edge about 60 miles south of Chicago. It was cut from Vermilion County in 1833, and Watseka, the county seat since 1865, is also the largest city. Gilman is the other city. The county covers 1,117 square miles of land, which ranks third in Illinois, with Kankakee County to the north, Vermilion to the south and Ford to the west.

Interstate 57 crosses the western side, passing near Chebanse, Clifton, Ashkum, Gilman, Onarga, Buckley and Loda, and U.S. Route 24 runs east and west through Gilman and Watseka. The 26 townships mean that a parcel's assessor depends on where it sits, so confirm the township on the bill.

QuickFacts, the Census Bureau's profile page, shows an estimated 26,150 residents as of July 2025, compared with 27,077 counted in 2020.

  • Housing units: 12,780, with 80.0 percent of occupied homes owned by the people living in them.
  • Middle-of-the-range value of a home that its owner lives in: $137,800 for 2020 to 2024, against a median gross rent of $799.
  • Median household income: $66,255, and a mean commute of 25.0 minutes.
  • Building permits issued in 2025: 14.

Adults 65 and older make up 24.9 percent of residents, so inherited and estate houses are a common reason owners here sell.

sections.h2: When are Iroquois County property taxes due?
sections.html:
The two installment dates are announced each year when bills are mailed, and they have moved around. The county's news releases give a first date in June in one year and in August in another. Treat the dates printed on your own bill as the rule, and expect a 1 1/2 percent penalty added for each month a balance stays unpaid.

Installment dates in two Iroquois County Treasurer news releases
Bills mailed forFirst installmentSecond installment
2021 taxes, payable 2022June 9September 9
2022 taxes, payable 2023August 18September 18

Bills carry two years, such as 2022 taxes payable 2023, so each bill is paid the year after its tax year. Ask the treasurer for a written payoff that shows every year with a balance, and give it to your title company.

Members of a United States Armed Forces Reserve unit called to active duty outside the continental United States may defer an installment until 180 days after returning, according to the same releases.

sections.h2: How can I pay an Iroquois County tax bill?
sections.html:
You can pay at the treasurer's office in Room 105, by mail, at a participating bank or online through the county's property tax search page. The online route asks for the parcel number without dashes, the owner name or the address, then a Pay Taxes button appears.

  • Card payments online carry a charge of 2.35 percent plus $1.50, and e-check payments carry $2.00.
  • Banks that collect taxes include 1st Trust and Savings Bank in Watseka and Clifton, Iroquois Federal, Iroquois Farmers State Bank, Prospect Bank, First State Bank of Forrest and Commonwealth Credit Union, among others on the treasurer's list.
  • A drop box near the 911 Center at the Administrative Center accepts payments after hours.
  • Send or bring the whole bill. The county's releases say a $1.00 fee applies to payments made without it, and a receipt requires the full bill, with a stamped envelope if mailed.

The county's 2023 release says mortgage companies must pay online by the due dates. If your lender escrows the tax, confirm which year it paid before you order a payoff.

sections.h2: How do I appeal an Iroquois County assessment?
sections.html:
A complaint goes to the Board of Review, and it must arrive no later than 30 days after your township's assessments are published. The board's 2026 rules say the deadline for each township is posted on its web page, and by state law the window cannot be stretched while you talk with a township assessor.

The board convenes on or before the first Monday in June and recesses from day to day as needed. A reduction takes effect only for the current assessment year, apart from omitted property. Everything you want considered must be filed with the complaint, because evidence sent later is not taken up.

  • Useful evidence includes an appraisal, comparable sales, a closing statement from a recent purchase and photographs.
  • Complaints on property owned by an LLC, partnership or corporation must be filed by an Illinois attorney.
  • After a hearing, either side may appeal to the Property Tax Appeal Board within 30 calendar days of the written decision, or file an objection in circuit court under 35 ILCS 200/23-5.

The assessment office explains that the board can raise or lower an assessment, and that values are reviewed on a four-year cycle. Assessments are set at one-third of fair cash value.

sections.h2: What exemptions can lower an Iroquois County bill?
sections.html:
The general homestead exemption removes up to $6,000 from the equalized assessed value of an owner-occupied home before tax is figured, under 35 ILCS 200/15-175. The county's 2026 application asks for a state driver's license or ID showing the home address, and after first approval the exemption renews automatically. If the house stops being your primary residence, you must have the exemption removed.

The Board of Review rules list the other homestead exemptions administered through the county:

  • Returning veterans, disabled persons and disabled veterans (sections 15-167 to 15-169).
  • Senior citizens over 65 (section 15-170) and the senior assessment freeze (section 15-172).
  • The homestead improvements exemption (section 15-180).

The assessment office advises that applications should reach it by December 31 of the assessment year so the bill is correct, and that the low-income senior freeze has a January 1 to July 1 filing window. The treasurer also publicizes a senior property tax deferral program that works as a loan with interest, repaid when the property is sold or after the owner's death. Ask for current terms, since any deferral comes due at a sale.

sections.h2: What happens if Iroquois County taxes go unpaid?
sections.html:
The treasurer's page carries tax sale buyer information and a buyer registration form, because unpaid parcels can be sold to a tax buyer at the annual sale. Buyers of tax certificates do not take your house at the sale. They gain a lien position and the right to petition for a deed if the owner never redeems.

State law now gives owners 3 years from the sale date to redeem property sold on certificates issued on or after January 1, 2024, with exceptions that begin with vacant property (35 ILCS 200/21-350). Redemption payments go to the county clerk. Ask the Iroquois County Clerk for the exact deadline and payoff on any parcel that was sold.

sections.h2: What should I settle before selling a house in Iroquois County?
sections.html:
Check the paper trail first, since county records and the closing date need to line up.

  • Pull the parcel record and confirm the owner name and mailing address with the assessment office.
  • Ask the treasurer for a payoff on every year that shows a balance.
  • Find out whether an exemption should come off the house after the sale.
  • Check whether a Board of Review complaint is open for your township.
  • Collect repair estimates if you plan to sell as is.

A cash buyer can purchase an Iroquois County house in its present condition, and any tax balance is cleared through the settlement at closing.

faqs.q: When is the Iroquois County property tax deadline?
faqs.a: The dates change each year and are printed on the bill. Past treasurer releases listed June 9 and September 9 for one year and August 18 and September 18 for another, with a 1 1/2 percent monthly penalty after each date.

faqs.q: Where do I pay property tax in Iroquois County?
faqs.a: Pay at the treasurer's office at 1001 East Grant Street in Watseka, by mail, at a participating county bank, through the online property tax search page or in the after-hours drop box.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to contest an Iroquois County assessment?
faqs.a: You have 30 days after the township's assessments are published. The Board of Review posts each township's filing deadline on its web page, and the window cannot be extended.

faqs.q: How much is the general homestead exemption in Iroquois County?
faqs.a: Qualified owners can remove up to $6,000 from the equalized assessed value under 35 ILCS 200/15-175. Apply at the Assessment Office in Room 106 with a driver's license or ID showing the home address.

faqs.q: Who do I call about Iroquois County taxes?
faqs.a: Call the Treasurer at (815) 432-6985 about bills and payments and the Assessment Office at (815) 432-6978 about values, exemptions and address changes. The County Clerk handles tax rates.
